points.title: The 41% Mirage
body: Roughly 41% of active Texas listings took a price cut recently.
That reads like panic. It isn't.
Most of those cuts came off a number that was never real to begin with.
points.loop: The first cut is never real.

points.title: Cut Twice, Sell Once
body: A home that cuts once usually cuts again inside a month.
By then buyers assume something is wrong with the house.
Pricing at the last real comp on day one beats two cuts every time.

points.title: Days On Market Lies
body: Plenty of listings get withdrawn and relisted so the counter starts over.
You see 6 days. The house has actually been sitting for 96.
Read the price history, not the days on market field.

points.title: Concessions Beat Cuts
body: Texas sellers are holding the sticker price and paying buyer costs instead.
Rate buydowns and closing credits are moving more money than price drops are.
It protects the comp for them and lowers the real cost for you.
points.loop: Most people time this wrong twice.

points.title: The Quiet Stretch
body: Buyers shop in spring, when they have the least leverage all year.
Sellers list in January because it feels fresh, then sit and wait.
The deals get made in the weeks nobody is paying attention.

linkedinCaption:
About 41% of active Texas listings have taken a price cut. That number gets read as a market in trouble. It usually means the first number was never grounded in a real comp.

A few things I'm watching right now.

Homes that cut once tend to cut again within a month, and by the second cut buyers assume there's a defect.

Days on market is unreliable. Withdrawn and relisted inventory resets the counter. The price history tells the truth.

More sellers are holding list price and paying buyer costs instead. Rate buydowns and closing credits are moving real money while protecting the comp.

And the best terms are rarely available in spring.

Are you seeing concessions outperform price reductions in your market too?
